extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing clear mathematical proofs using direct proof, case analysis, contrapositive, contradiction, and for producing good mathematical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conditional statement If P, then Q, assume P and use logic and definitions to deduce Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the proof with the assumption P (e.g., 'Suppose P.') and then derive Q. It can help to work backwards from Q to something obviously true, then reverse steps; map out a strategy; use previously proved propositions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using cases (case analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement's truth depends on different possibilities, examine each case and prove the statement in all possible scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition the possibilities (e.g., n even or odd) and handle each separately. Use explicit case headings (Case 1, Case 2, ...). If two cases behave the same except for a minor swap, consider treating them similarly (see 'Treating similar cases').

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating similar cases / WLOG
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more cases are nearly identical, it is appropriate to write out just one and indicate that the others are similar, often with the phrase 'Without loss of generality...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors recommend avoiding the abbreviation 'WLOG' for transparency; until experienced, write out all cases even if similar. Use 'Without loss of generality, suppose ...' to indicate you're treating one representative case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive proof (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove If P, then Q, prove the logically equivalent contrapositive ∼Q ⇒ ∼P: assume ∼Q and deduce ∼P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First line typically 'Suppose Q is not true.' Last line 'Therefore P is not true.' Use logic and possibly direct proof to transform ∼Q to ∼P. Remember contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original conditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a proposition P, assume ∼P and deduce a contradiction (some C ∧ ∼C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin 'Suppose for the sake of contradiction that ∼P.' Work from ∼P until you deduce an outright false statement (e.g., 1 is even and 1 is odd) or any clear contradiction. For conditional If P then Q, assume P and ∼Q and derive a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating quantified/compound statements (use DeMorgan etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using contrapositive or contradiction you must correctly form negations of statements, including quantifiers and compound statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply DeMorgan’s laws (e.g., ∼(A and B) = ∼A or ∼B, ∼∀x P(x) = ∃x ∼P(x)). Use these rules to unpack negations properly and to convert ∼(P⇒Q) into useful assumptions (for conditionals, P and ∼Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing proof technique pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the proof method (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases) that makes the argument flow more easily given the nature of P and Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if isolating variables from a complicated expression is hard, contrapositive may simplify; if goal naturally follows from assuming ∼Q, use contrapositive; if assuming ∼P leads quickly to nonsense, use contradiction. It's normal to combine techniques inside a single proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining techniques / nested proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs often require combining methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, case analysis) and may contain smaller proofs inside a larger proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overall approach can be direct, while proving a subclaim might best use contradiction or contrapositive. Be explicit about transitions between techniques and keep inner proofs clearly demarcated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting proofs with a clear assumption line
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin proofs by explicitly stating the assumption you will work from (e.g., 'Suppose x and y are positive real numbers.' or 'Suppose ∼Q.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarity signals the chosen method and gives readers a clear starting point. For contradiction/contrapositive, phrase the opening line to reflect that strategy ('Suppose for the sake of contradiction...' or 'Suppose Q is not true.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify algebraic/inequality-preserving operations
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying operations that can change inequalities or other relations (e.g., taking square roots), justify that the operation preserves the relation under the current hypotheses (e.g., both sides nonnegative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use previously proved propositions or explicit hypotheses (like positivity) to justify steps such as taking square roots or dividing by positive numbers. Do not apply operations that may reverse inequalities without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition cases to obtain existence/constructive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving existential statements that depend on sign or parity, construct the required witness by cases (e.g., produce n for each possibility of a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly handle subcases like zero/positive/negative when constructing examples (as in showing every multiple of 4 equals 1 + (−1)^n(2n−1) for some n). Ensure each branch produces the required witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of definitions to drive divisibility/congruence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: For divisibility and congruence proofs, start from the definition (n | a means a = nk) and manipulate algebraically to show the desired divisibility or congruence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply both sides, factor, or introduce integer multipliers as needed. Explicitly state the integer introduced (e.g., 'there exists k ∈ Z such that ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Explaining new symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Every new symbol introduced in a proof must have its meaning explained to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you write b = ac, clarify 'for some integer c' rather than leaving c unexplained. This prevents readers from searching backwards for the origin of symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin sentences with words, not symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should start with a word rather than a mathematical symbol to avoid ambiguity caused by case sensitivity and to conform to normal capitalization rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite 'x is an integer, so 2x+5 is an integer' as 'Because x is an integer, 2x + 5 is an integer.' Avoid starting sentences with bare symbols like 'x^2 − x + 2 = 0 has two solutions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: End sentences with a period, even if they end in a mathematical expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat mathematical statements as parts of sentences and use normal punctuation; end with a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Write 'Euler proved that 
∑_{p ∈ P} 1/(1 − 1/p^s).' with a period at the end. This preserves sentence structure and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate mathematical symbols/expressions with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words to separate mathematical expressions so they don't run together and cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'Because x^2 − 1 = 0, it follows that x = 1 or x = −1.' over 'Because x^2 − 1 = 0, x = 1 or x = −1.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse and overuse of symbols in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols like =, ≤, ∈, ⊆, etc., belong in mathematical expressions, not as substitutes for words in ordinary prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'Since the two sets are equal, one is a subset of the other.' rather than 'Since the two sets are =, one is a subset of the other.' Avoid unnecessary symbolic clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include symbols where plain words suffice; unnecessary notation muddies exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'No set has negative cardinality.' over 'No set X has negative cardinality.' when the extra symbol offers no purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person plural and active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical writing commonly uses 'we' and active constructions to guide the reader through arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'Dividing both sides by 5, we get x = 3.' to a passive or impersonal phrasing. This makes proofs more engaging and clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch out for ambiguous pronouns ('it')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pronouns like 'it' when their antecedent could be unclear; name the object explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'we see that it is not empty' with 'we see that Y is not empty' to remove ambiguity about whether 'it' refers to X or Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical connective words carefully ('since', 'because', 'so', 'for')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'since', 'because', 'so' assert both the premise and its consequence; ensure their use matches what you mean (assertion vs. conditional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the difference between 'If P then Q' and the constructions 'Since P, Q' (which assert P is true). Use them only when appropriate to avoid implying unintended assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conclusion adverbs correctly ('therefore', 'hence', 'thus')
rubrics_metrics.description: Words such as 'therefore' and 'hence' should be used immediately before a statement that logically follows from previous sentences or clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the statement following these adverbs indeed follows; don't use them where the logical connection is missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity is the gold standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When rules conflict with clarity, prioritize making the argument clearer even if that means breaking a stylistic rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical writing evolves with practice; read other people's proofs and adopt what makes exposition clearer. Explicitness is encouraged especially for learners.
